summary: Isle La Motte Light, on a Lake Champlain island in Vermont, has a 1881 cast-iron tower that was dark from 1933 to 2002 and is now a private, closed residence and an active aid.

lens.where: original sixth-order lens; later light not described

structures.type: conical cast-iron tower on concrete crib
structures.note: 25 ft to lantern; light 46 ft above water (LighthouseFriends; USLHS)

structures.type: steel skeleton tower with automatic beacon
structures.note: Erected 1933; described as deteriorating in 2001 (LighthouseFriends). Current state not checked.

access.note: Privately owned residence; closed to the public. Visitors are asked not to enter the grounds or approach the tower (Vermonter).

events.note: First light: lantern displayed from a window, or hung from a pine tree and moved to a window (sources differ on location)
Collector of customs at Plattsburgh recommends $5,000 for a lighthouse on the northern end of the island
Federal government buys a parcel of land on the island for $50
Lantern mounted on a small stone pyramid (Vermonter); limestone tower with lens lantern (LighthouseFriends); tended by a local farmer

Light-House Board's 1868 report: the light is 'not to be relied on' in stormy nights, and it proposes a dwelling with a lantern on top (LighthouseFriends). Vermonter says a small keeper's house was added that year. Not settled from the sources read.
Authorization for a permanent lighthouse granted
Local landowner disputes title to the lighthouse lot; the Board refuses
25-ft cast-iron tower and detached keeper's cottage; light first exhibited by Keeper Wilbur F. Hill
Sixth-order Fresnel lens, fixed white, focal plane 46 ft
Steps built from the shore to the top of the hill; various repairs (Light-House Board)
Brick oil house added to the station
Keeper Hill commended for towing ashore a disabled boat with three people (LighthouseFriends); listed in the FY1915 saving-of-life table
William W. Grant arrives 18 April 1919 after Hill's death in March
Steel skeleton tower with automatic beacon erected; light automated at the end of June 1933
Old tower's light discontinued (USLHS Year Discontinued 1933-2002)
Lighthouse acquired by a private family
Coast Guard considers replacing the deteriorating steel tower and decides to return the light to the original tower
Light restored to active service in the original tower on 5 October 2002, before a crowd of over 300

keepers.name: Wilbur Fisk Hill
keepers.note: Began at the old pyramid light in 1871; first exhibited the iron-tower light in 1881; retired end of January 1919 at 76 (LighthouseFriends); died 19 March 1919. Named in the FY1915 Commissioner's table as W. F. Hill.

keepers.name: William W. Grant
keepers.note: Arrived 18 April 1919 after an engineer's career on lighthouse tenders; allowed to remain after automation until the station was sold (LighthouseFriends).

corrections.why: The cast-iron tower and its keeper's cottage were authorized in 1879 and first lit in 1881 (USLHS Year Tower Established 1881; LighthouseFriends). The 1856 date belongs to the earlier stone pyramid or limestone tower on the site, which the record's cast-iron tower entry conflates with the later tower.

The light was returned to active service in its original tower on 5 October 2002 (LighthouseFriends; USLHS 'Active Aid to Navigation?: Yes'). The record's 2002 entry describes a relighting, not a deactivation.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Coast Guard date (1829) is used, from the Vermonter article and the USLHS 'Year Established: 1829'. Sources differ on where the first light hung: a window of a house (Vermonter), or a pine tree moved to a window (LighthouseFriends). Both are given in the story.

notes_for_editor: (1) The 1829 first light: LighthouseFriends says a lantern hung from a pine tree and was moved to a window; Vermonter says a lantern was displayed from a window. Both given. (2) The 1856-57 structure: LighthouseFriends describes a limestone tower with a lens lantern, 18.5 ft; Vermonter describes a small stone pyramid with a lantern on top, lit 1857. The station record's 'tower, crib, cast_iron, built 1856' conflates the two; see corrections. (3) Hill and the FY1915 table: the table is OCR'd and its columns were read by position. 'W. F. Hill, keeper, Isle La Motte Light Station, Vt.' is taken from the table row. The table's neighbouring vessel-assistance entries (for example a power boat with six people towed to Plattsburgh) are not matched to Hill; the three-person rescue is LighthouseFriends' account only. Check the page image (scan 65, printed 60). (4) Private residents: LighthouseFriends names the family that bought the station in 1949 and their relatives, and the seller. None are named in the story: they are private residents of a converted lighthouse, and the owners' public role is not evident in the sources. (5) The 1928 Grant description: LighthouseFriends does not name its source; it is cited to LighthouseFriends only and short. (6) No newspapers were searched for this station (the search budget went to the other two). Gaps: the 1933 automation, the 1949 sale and the 2002 relighting have no newspaper cross-check; Vermont papers in Chronicling America (for example Burlington or St. Albans) could be searched. (7) The steel skeleton tower's present state is unknown (LighthouseFriends says deteriorating in 2001). (8) Wikipedia is lead-only and was not cited. (9) The current optic on the USLHS record (300 mm) and the station record's Fl W 4s characteristic were not checked against the Coast Guard Light List. (10) The 1891 Light-House Board entry is OCR-garbled ('vrious'); the quote is kept as OCR'd. (11) Page-read budget: about 6 web reads plus corpus; within the guide's 15. (12) Fact-check pass, 2026-10-28: the story no longer calls LighthouseFriends' limestone tower and Vermonter's 1857 stone pyramid 'the same structure'; it gives each source's description with its own citation. The FY1915 Hill entry is read from the 'Saving of life and property' table row ('W. F. Hill, keeper, Isle La Motte Light Station, Vt.'), which is on the same OCR line as the name and station; the table's vessel-aided column is separate, and the story does not link Hill to any vessel. The scanned page image was not opened. The 1868 keeper's house disagreement (LighthouseFriends says a dwelling was proposed; Vermonter says a keeper's house was added that year) is recorded in the event note and is not in the story. The 1891 quotation keeps the OCR 'vrious' and the story does not quote it.
